newsitem.title: FRANCE: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE SEEKING LANDMARK WIN FOR WILLIAMS.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-VILLENEUVE SEEKING LANDMARK WIN FOR WILLIAMS.

text.p: Jacques Villeneuve will be looking not only for a revival of his own fortunes but also a landmark victory for Williams in Sunday's French Grand Prix.
Success at the Magny-Cours track would provide Williams with their 100th Grand Prix win, closing the gap on all-time leaders Ferrari and McLaren who have 110 and 105 wins respectively.

The 26-year-old Canadian, the early season championship leader, has been overtaken by Michael Schumacher of Germany, winner in his Ferrari in Montreal two weeks ago when Villeneuve suffered the embarrassment of crashing out in front of his home fans.
Villeneuve was fastest by a very fine margin in testing last week and knows his Williams car's performance can be matched by several of his rivals.
Schumacher was another who tested well in France last week but the biggest threat to Villeneuve's hopes could come from Frenchman Jean Alesi in a Benetton.

Alesi was consistently fast through both recent test sessions in France and has high hopes of scoring his first win since joining Benetton from Ferrari -- as Schumacher's replacement -- at the end of 1995.
"We have done a lot of good work, the car is in good condition and our modifications have all worked well," he said.
"I have been on the podium at the last two races, finishing third and then second, so, of course, I am confident and optimistic for this race."

Alesi and Benetton have struggled since he arrived in the wake of Schumacher's departure but there have been signs in the last month that the team has overcome its difficulties and is starting to regain the reliability, consistency and team-work standards which took them to both the drivers' and constructors' titles in 1995.

"I have a feeling that we are round the corner and, with a little bit of luck, we could soon be back in a good groove," said technical director Pat Symonds. "But I would not want to tempt providence by suggesting we can win the French Grand Prix."
Schumacher leads the title race with 37 points with Villeneuve on 30 and Olivier Panis of France third on 15.
Panis, who crashed and suffered double fractures to both legs in Montreal, will watch the race at home with his family in Brittany after flying back from Canada this week.

His place in the Prost team has been taken by 22-year-old Italian Jarno Trulli who has been released by the Minardi team. Minardi are backed by Benetton's managing director Italian Flavio Briatore who is also the former owner of Ligier and manager of Trulli.

It is expected that Trulli's place at Minardi will be taken Argentine youngster Tarso Marques while fellow-Argentine Norberto Fontana will take over from another injured driver, Italian Gianni Morbidelli, who broke his left arm in testing last week, in the Sauber team.

These two accidents will intensify the attention paid to safety at the French Grand Prix, the oldest event in top-level motor sport with a history dating back to 1906. Since then, the race has been held at many circuits in France including Rheims, Clermont-Ferrand, Le Castellet and Dijon.

It has been held at Magny-Cours, situated in central France midway between Paris and Lyon, for the last five years. The track is one of the smoothest and most technical on the calendar and puts the onus on taking each of the rare overtaking opportunities that arise.
